title: Sick child, age 2 months up to 5 years

convulsingNow.title: Convulsing now (stabilized, the consultation continues)
convulsingNow.description: The child is convulsing now --> Treat immediately

convulsions.title: Convulsions in this illness
convulsions.description:
The child has had one or more convulsions.
During a convulsion, the child’s arms and legs stiffen because the muscles are contracting. The child may lose consciousness or cannot respond to spoken directions. Use words the caregiver understands. For example, the caregiver may call convulsions “fits” or “spasms”.

convulsionCount.title: Number of convulsions in this illness

convulsionLong.title: A convulsion lasted 15 minutes or longer
convulsionLong.description: The child has had one or more convulsions lasting 15 minutes or longer.

lethargic.title: Unconscious or lethargic
lethargic.description: A lethargic child is not awake and alert when they should be. The child is drowsy and does not show interest in what is happening around them.

notAbleToDrink.title: Not able to drink or breastfeed
notAbleToDrink.description: A child shows signs of not being able to drink or breastfeed if they are not able to suck or swallow when offered a drink or breast-milk.

vomitsEverything.title: Vomiting everything
vomitsEverything.description: The child is reported to be vomiting everything (not able to hold anything down at all).

oralFluidTest.title: Oral fluid test result
oralFluidTest.description: Do not do the test if the child is unconscious.

feverReported.title: Fever reported (fever in this illness)
feverReported.description: The child has "Fever reported" (history of fever) if the child has had any fever with this illness.

axillaryTemperature.title: Axillary temperature (°C)
axillaryTemperature.description: The child's axillary temperature (temperature taken under the armpit), measured in °C.

rectalTemperature.title: Rectal temperature (°C)
rectalTemperature.description: Only if trained to take it.

thermometerNotAvailable.title: No thermometer available
thermometerNotAvailable.description: A thermometer is not available to measure the child's temperature.

hotToTouch.title: Hot to touch
hotToTouch.description: The child is hot to touch.

travelToHighRiskArea.title: Travel to a high malaria risk area in the last 2 weeks
travelToHighRiskArea.description: The child has recently travelled (in the last 2 weeks) to a high malaria risk area.

feverDuration.title: Fever for how long?
feverDuration.description:
Length of time the child has had fever
- 7 days or less (1 week or less)
- More than 7 days (more than 1 week)

feverEveryDay.title: Fever present every day for more than 7 days?
feverEveryDay.description: If the fever has been present for more than 7 days, ask if the fever has been present every day. A fever that has been present every day for more than 7 days can mean that the child has a more severe disease, such as typhoid fever. The child will need referral for further assessment.

stiffNeck.title: Stiff neck
stiffNeck.description:
A stiff neck may be a sign of meningitis, cerebral malaria or another very severe febrile disease. It requires urgent treatment with injectable antibiotics and referral to a hospital.
WATCH THE CHILD: While you talk with the caregiver during the assessment, look to see if the child moves and bends their neck easily when looking around. If the child is moving and bending their neck, the child does not have a stiff neck.
TEST THE CHILD: If you did not see any movement, or if you are not sure, draw the child’s attention to their umbilicus or toes. For example, you can shine a flashlight on the toes or umbilicus or tickle the toes to encourage the child to look down. Look to see if the child can bend their neck when looking down at their umbilicus or toe.
FEEL FOR A STIFF NECK:If you still have not seen the child bend their  neck , ask the caregiver to help you lay the child on their back. Lean over the child, and gently support the child’s back and shoulders with one hand. With the other hand, hold the child’s head. Then carefully bend the head forward towards the child’s chest. If the neck bends easily, the child does not have a stiff neck. If the neck feels stiff and there is resistance to bending, the child has a stiff neck. Often a child with a stiff neck will cry when you try to bend the neck.

refusalToUseLimb.title: Refusal to use a limb
refusalToUseLimb.description: The child is unable to use a limb (arm or leg) on examination. It is important to assess for refusal to use a limb, which could be a sign of a bone or joint infection when the child has reported or measured fever.

warmTenderJoint.title: Warm, tender or swollen joint or bone
warmTenderJoint.description: The child has a warm, tender or swollen joint or bone, which could be a sign of a infection when the child has reported or measured fever.

painPassingUrine.title: Pain or difficulty passing urine, or crying when passing urine
painPassingUrine.description: The child is reported to have or appears to have pain or difficulty passing urine (in younger children this may appear as crying when passing urine).

cough.title: Cough
cough.description: The caregiver reports that the child has a cough, or you see that the child has a cough.

runnyNose.title: Runny nose
runnyNose.description: The child has a runny nose.

redEyes.title: Red eyes
redEyes.description: The child has “red eyes” if there is redness in the white part of the eye. In a healthy eye, the white part of the eye is clearly white and not discoloured.

otherSevereClassification.title: Severe classification from another part of the assessment
otherSevereClassification.description: For example severe pneumonia, mastoiditis or complicated severe acute malnutrition. This demo does not have those parts.

malariaTest.title: Malaria test result
malariaTest.description: unknown: status unknown, test unavailable, invalid or not feasible

highParasiteDensity.title: High parasite density
highParasiteDensity.description: P. falciparum more than 10% or 500 000 per microlitre, or P. knowlesi more than 2% or 100 000 per microlitre

skinProblem.title: Skin problem
skinProblem.description:
A generalized skin problem is a skin problem that affects the whole body, a large area of the body or several parts of the body, whereas a localized skin problem is limited to one area of the body.
This question is prompted either if a skin problem has been noted already, or if the child has fever with one or more of cough, runny nose or red eyes (to assess for measles)

measlesRash.title: Measles rash
measlesRash.description: In measles, a rash begins behind the ears and on the neck. It spreads to the face. During the next day, the rash spreads to the rest of the body, arms and legs. After 4–5 days, the rash starts to fade and the skin may peel.

measlesRecent.title: Measles within the last 3 months
measlesRecent.description: Ask the caregiver or check the child's health record to see if they have had measles in the last 3 months. If the caregiver is not sure, explain the symptoms (a generalized rash all over the body, starting from behind the ears and on the neck, spreading to the face, then the body, arms and legs, accompanied by a runny nose, red eyes or cough).

mouthUlcers.title: Oral sores or mouth ulcers
mouthUlcers.description: Examination for oral sores or mouth ulcers should be carried out at the end of the physical examination so as not to upset or aggitate the child before completing other physical examinations.

pusFromEye.title: Pus draining from the eye
pusFromEye.description:
Pus draining from the eye is a sign of conjunctivitis. Conjunctivitis is an infection of the conjunctiva, the inside surface of the eyelid and the white part of the eye.
If you do not see pus draining from the eye, look for pus on the conjunctiva or on the eyelids. Often the pus forms a crust when the child is sleeping and seals the eye shut. You can gently open the eye, making sure that your hands are clean.
Wash your hands after examining the eye of any child with pus draining from the eye.

corneaClouding.title: Clouding of the cornea
corneaClouding.description:
The cornea is usually clear. When clouding of the cornea is present, the cornea may appear clouded or hazy. The cornea may look the way a glass of water looks when you add a small amount of milk. Clouding may occur in one or both eyes.
A child with corneal clouding may keep their eyes tightly shut when exposed to light. The light may cause irritation and pain to the child’s eyes. To check the child’s eyes, wait for the child to open their eye or gently pull down the lower eyelid to look for clouding.
Corneal clouding is a dangerous condition. It may be the result of vitamin A deficiency that has been made worse by measles. If corneal clouding is not treated, the cornea can ulcerate and cause blindness. A child with clouding of the cornea needs urgent treatment with vitamin A.

vitaminARecent.title: Vitamin A, or malnutrition treatment that contains vitamin A, in the past month
